20	For ease of notation we extensively use the subscript range notation.
    21	For example, if $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_\ell$ are fixed subspaces of $V$ and $k \in
    22	\{1, 2, \ldots, \ell\}$ we write
    23	\begin{equation*}
    24	  V_{<k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,1 \le j<k} V_j\;,\quad
    25	  V_{> k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\, \ell\ge j > k} V_j\;,
    26	\end{equation*}
    27	and it is understood that $V_{\le k}$ and $V_{\ge k}$ are identical to
    28	$V_{<k+1}$ and $V_{>k-1}$, respectively.
    29	Moreover, if $V'$ is a register subspace of $V$, $F: V' \to V'$ is a function,
    30	and $x \in V$, we write $x^F$ to denote $F(x^{V'})$.
    31	For example, in the following definition $x^{L_1}$ is used as shorthand notation
    32	for $L_1(x^{V_1})$.
    33	
    34	
    35	\begin{definition}
    36	  \label{def:cl-func}
    37		Let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some $n\geq 0$.
    38	  For all integers $\ell\geq 0$ the collection of \emph{$\ell$-level
    39	    conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is defined
    40	  inductively as follows.
    41	  \begin{enumerate}
    42	  \item There is a single $0$-level conditionally linear function, which is the
    43	    $0$ function on $V$.
    44	
    45	  \item Let $\ell \geq 1$ and suppose the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level
    46	    conditionally linear functions has been defined.
    47	    The collection of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions on $V$ consists
    48	    of all functions $L$ on $V$ that can be expressed in the following form.
    49	    There exist complementary register subspaces $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ of $V$, a
    50	    linear function $L_1$ on $V_1$, and for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$, an
    51	    $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear function $L_{>1,\, v}$ on $V_{>1}$,
    52	    such that for all $x\in V$,
    53	    \begin{equation*}
    54	      L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}} (x^{V_{>1}})\;.
    55	    \end{equation*}
    56	  \end{enumerate}
    57	\end{definition}
    58	
    59	The concept of conditionally linear functions is simple even though the
    60	notations seem complicated.
    61	It is best understood using an operational definition illustrated in
    62	\cref{fig:cl-functions}.
    63	We give an example of a $2$-level CL function in \cref{ex:cl-function}.
    64	
    65	\begin{remark}
    66	  \label{rk:level-1-is-linear}
    67	  It follows from the above definition that all $1$-level CL functions are linear.
    68	\end{remark}
    69	
    70	\begin{example}\label{ex:cl-function}
    71	Consider $V = \F_{2}^{3}$. Then the following map
    72	\begin{equation*}
    73	  L:(x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2})
    74	  \mapsto (0, x_{0}x_{2} + x_{1}x_{2} + x_{0},  x_{2})
    75	\end{equation*}
    76	on $V$ is a $2$-level CL function by choosing $V_{1} = \mathrm{span}\{(0,0,1)\}$, $L_{1}$
    77	the identity function on $V_{1}$, $V_{2} = V_{1}^{\perp}$, and
    78	\begin{equation*}
    79	  L_{2,\, x_{2}}: (x_{0}, x_{1}, 0)
    80	  \mapsto (0, x_{0}x_{2} + x_{1}x_{2} + x_{0}, 0),
    81	\end{equation*}
    82	which is linear for all $x_{2} \in \F_{2}$.
    83	Note that intuitively the function $L$ selects either $x_{0}$ or $x_{1}$ in the
    84	second coordinate conditioning on the value of $x_{2}$.
    85	\end{example}

   122	\begin{remark}
   123	  \label{rk:higher-level}
   124	  Note that for any integer $\ell\geq 1$ the collection of $\ell$-level CL
   125	  functions trivially contains the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level CL functions:
   126	  for this it suffices to note that the $0$ function, which is a $0$-level CL
   127	  function, is also a $1$-level CL function by setting $V_1=V$, $V_{>1}= \{0\}$,
   128	  $L_1(x)=0$ for all $x\in V$, and $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ is the $0$ map for all
   129	  $x\in V$.

   132	\begin{definition}
   133	  \label{def:cl-dist}
   134	  Let $L, R: V \to V$ be conditionally linear functions.
   135	  The \emph{conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ corresponding to $(L,
   136	    R)$} is defined as the distribution over pairs $(L(x), R(x)) \in V \times V$
   137	  for $x$ drawn uniformly at random from $V$.
   138	\end{definition}
   139	
   140	Throughout the paper we abbreviate ``conditionally linear functions'' and
   141	``conditionally linear distributions'' as \emph{CL functions} and \emph{CL
   142	  distributions}, respectively.
   143	
   144	The following lemma elucidates structural properties of $\ell$-level CL
   145	functions.
   146	Recall that using our shorthand notation, $x^{L_{<k}}$ and $x^{L_k}$ in the
   147	lemma denote $L_{<k}(x)$ and $L_{k,u}(x^{V_{k,\, u}})$ where $u = L_{<k}(x)$.
   148	
   149	
   150	\begin{lemma}
   151	  \label{lem:cl-kth}
   152		Let $\ell \geq 1$ and $V = \F^n$ for some integer $n \geq 0$.
   153	  A function $L: V \to V$ is an $\ell$-level CL function if and only if the
   154	  following collection of functions and subspaces exists:
   155	  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
   156	  \item \label{enu:cl-k-marginal} For each $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, \ell\}$, a
   157	    function $L_{\le k} : V \to V$ called the \emph{$k$-th marginal of $L$};
   158	  \item \label{enu:cl-k-space} For each $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, \ell\}$ and $u
   159	    \in L_{<k} (V)$, a register subspace $V_{k,\, u}$ of $V$ called the
   160	    \emph{$k$-th factor space with prefix $u$};
   161	  \item \label{enu:cl-k-map} For each $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, \ell\}$ and $u \in
   162	    L_{<k} (V)$, a linear map $L_{k,\, u} : V_{k,\, u} \to V_{k,\, u}$ called
   163	    the \emph{$k$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix $u$};
   164	  \end{enumerate}
   165	  such that the following conditions hold for all $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots,
   166	  \ell\}$.
   167	  \begin{enumerate}
   168	  \item \label{enu:cl-k-cl} $L_{\leq k}$ is a $k$-level CL function on $V$;
   169		\item \label{enu:cl-space-sum} $V = \bigoplus_{i = 1}^\ell V_{i,\,
   170	      x^{L_{<i}}}$ for all $x \in V$;
   171	\item \label{enu:cl-map-sum} $L_{\leq k}(x) = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} x^{L_i}$ for
   172	    all $x \in V$, where $L_i$ is shorthand notation for $L_{i,\,
   173	      x^{L_{<i}}}$;
   174	  \item \label{enu:cl-last-ell} $L = L_{\leq \ell}$.
   175	  \end{enumerate}
   176	  As in \cref{enu:cl-map-sum}, we sometimes use $V_k$ and $L_k$ to denote
   177	  $V_{k,\, u}$ and $L_{k,\, u}$ respectively, leaving the prefix $u$ implicit.
   178	\end{lemma}
   179	
   180	\begin{proof}
   181		We first prove the ``if'' direction: if there exist spaces and functions
   182	  satisfying the conditions in the lemma, the fact that $L$ is an $\ell$-level
   183	  CL function follows from \cref{enu:cl-k-cl,enu:cl-last-ell} of the lemma
   184	  statement.
   185	
   186	  We now prove the ``only if'' direction.
   187	  Given a CL function $L$ on $V$, we construct the $k$-th family of subspaces
   188	  and functions for all $k \in \{1, \ldots, \ell\}$ by induction on the level
   189	  $\ell$.
   190	  First consider the base case $\ell=1$.
   191	  Since $L_{<1} = 0$, we omit the mentioning of the prefix $u \in L_{<1}(V)$.
   192	  Define $L_{\leq 1} = L$, the factor space $V_1 = V$, and the linear map $L_1 =
   193	  L$.
   194	  It is straightforward to verify that the conditions in the lemma hold for
   195	  these choices of linear maps and spaces.
   196	  
   197	  Now, assume that the lemma holds for CL functions of level at most $\ell - 1$,
   198	  and we prove the lemma for $\ell$-level CL functions.
   199	  By definition, an $\ell$-level CL function $L$ can be written as
   200	  \begin{equation*}
   201	  	L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})
   202	  \end{equation*}
   203	  for some linear map $L_1 : V_1 \to V_1$ and a family of $(\ell-1)$-level CL
   204	  functions
   205	  \begin{equation*}
   206	    \bigl \{ L_{>1,\, v} : V_{>1} \to V_{>1} \bigr \}_{\, v \in L_1(V_1)}
   207	  \end{equation*}
   208	  where $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ are complementary register subspaces of $V$.
   209	  Next, using the inductive hypothesis on the $(\ell-1)$-level CL function
   210	  $L_{>1,\, v}$ we get that for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$ and all $k \in \{1, 2,
   211	  \ldots, \ell-1\}$ there exist $k$-th marginal functions $L'_{v,\, \le k}:
   212	  V_{>1} \to V_{>1}$, $k$-th factor spaces $V'_{v,\, k,\, u}$, and $k$-th linear
   213	  maps $L'_{v,\, k,\, u}$ of $L_{>1,\, v}$ with prefix $u \in L'_{v,\,
   214	    <k}(V_{>1})$ such that the conditions of the lemma for $L_{>1,\, v}$ hold.
   215	  
   216	  Define the marginal functions $L_{\le k} : V \to V$, factor spaces
   217	  $V_{k,\, u}$ and linear maps $L_{k,\, u}$ for $L$ as follows.
   218	  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
   219	  \item Define $L_{\le 1} = L_1$ and the first factor space to be $V_1$;
   220	  \item For all $k \in \{2, 3, \ldots, \ell\}$, define
   221	    \begin{equation}
   222	      \label{eq:cl-k-def}
   223	      L_{\le k}: x \mapsto x^{L_1} + L'_{x^{L_1},\, <k} (x^{V_{>1}})
   224	      \quad\text{for } x\in V;
   225	    \end{equation}
   226		\item For all $k \in \{2, 3, \ldots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{< k}(V)$, define
   227	    $V_{k,\, u} = V'_{v,\, k-1,\, w}$ and $L_{k,\, u} = L'_{v,\, k-1,\, w}$
   228	    where $v = u^{V_1} \in L_{1}(V_{1})$ and $w = u^{V_{>1}} \in L'_{v,< k-1}(V_{> 1})$.
   229	  \end{enumerate}
   230	  We verify that the conditions of the lemma are satisfied.
   231	  Since $L'_{v,\, < k}$ is by assumption a $(k-1)$-level CL function on $V_{>
   232	    1}$, we get that $L_{\leq k}$ is a $k$-level CL function on $V$ from
   233	  \cref{eq:cl-k-def}, establishing \cref{enu:cl-k-cl}.
   234	  By the induction hypothesis, we have for all $v\in L_1(V_1)$ and $y \in
   235	  V_{>1}$,
   236	  \begin{equation}
   237	    \label{eq:cl-k-1}
   238	    V_{>1} = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell-1}
   239	    V'_{\smash{v,\, i, \, y^{L'_{v,\, <i}}}},
   240	  \end{equation}
   241	  which implies that for all $x \in V$ and $v = x^{L_1}$,
   242	  \begin{equation*}
   243	    V = V_1 \oplus \Big ( \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell-1}
   244	    V'_{\smash{v,\, i, \, x^{L'_{v,\, <i}}}} \Big)
   245	    = V_1 \oplus \Big (\bigoplus_{i=2}^{\ell} V_{i,\, x^{L_{<i}}} \Big)
   246	    = \bigoplus_{i=1}^\ell V_{i,\, x^{L_{<i}}}\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  The first equality follows from \cref{eq:cl-k-1} while the second and third
   249	  equalities follow from the definition of $V_{k,\, u}$.
   250	  This establishes \cref{enu:cl-space-sum}.
   251	
   252	  Next, we have that for all $x \in V$, $v = x^{L_1}$, and $k \in
   253	  \{1,2,\ldots,\ell\}$,
   254	  \begin{align}
   255	    \label{eq:cl-last-ell}
   256	    L_{\leq k}(x)
   257	    & = v + L'_{v,\, <k} (x^{V_{>1}}) \\
   258	    & = v + \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} x^{L'_{v,\, i}}
   259	    = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} x^{L_{i}}, \label{eq:cl-last-ell2}
   260	  \end{align}
   261	  where $L'_{v,\, i}$ is the $i$-th linear map of $L_{>1,\, v}$ with prefix
   262	  $L'_{v,\, <i}(x)$ and $L_i$ is the $i$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix
   263	  $L_{<i}(x)$.
   264	  The second equality follows from the inductive hypothesis applied to $L'_{v,\,
   265	    <k}$ and the third equality follows from the definition of $L_{i}$.
   266	  Line~\eqref{eq:cl-last-ell2} implies \cref{enu:cl-map-sum} of the lemma.
   267	  
   268	  Finally, \Cref{enu:cl-last-ell} follows from~\eqref{eq:cl-last-ell} where we
   269	  set $k = \ell$ and observe that $L'_{x^{L_1},\, \le \ell-1}$ is equal to
   270	  $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ by the inductive hypothesis.
   271	  This shows that $L_{\le k}$, $V_{k,\, u}$, and $L_{k,\, u}$ satisfy the
   272	  conditions of the lemma and completes the induction.
   273	\end{proof}
   274	
   275	We note that the marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given
   276	CL function $L$ may not be unique; for example, consider the identity function
   277	on a linear space $V = \F^n$.
   278	This is clearly a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a
   279	$k$-level CL function for $k \in \{2, \ldots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition
   280	of $V$ into factor spaces.
   281	
   282	\begin{lemma}
   283	  \label{lem:cl-concat}
   284	  Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces.
   285	  Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   286	  function on $V$ for each $u \in L(U)$.
   287	  Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$ defined as
   288	  \begin{equation*}
   289	    T (x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)} (x^V)
   290	  \end{equation*}
   291	  is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U\oplus V$.
   292	\end{lemma}
   293	
   294	\begin{proof}
   295	  We prove the claim by induction on $k$.
   296	  The case $k = 0$ follows from the Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   297	  Assume that the lemma holds for $L$ being at most $(k-1)$-level.
   298	  By Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, there are complementary register subspaces
   299	  $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$, a linear function $L_1$ on $U_1$, and a family of
   300	  $(k-1)$-level CL functions $L_{>1,\, v}$ for $v \in L_1(U_1)$ such that
   301	  \begin{equation*}
   302	    L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}).
   303	  \end{equation*}
   304	  For all $x^{L_1}$, define the function $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ on $U_{>1} \oplus V$ as
   305	  \begin{equation*}
   306	    T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1} \oplus V}) = L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}) +
   307	    R_{x^{L_1} + x^{L_{>1}}}(x^V),
   308	  \end{equation*}
   309	  the concatenation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ and $\{ R_{L(x^U)} \}_{x^{L_{>1}}}$
   310	  where $L_{>1}$ is the shorthand notation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$.
   311	  By the induction hypothesis, $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ is $(k+\ell-1)$-level
   312	  conditionally linear.
   313	  The lemma follows from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   314	\end{proof}
   315	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of CL functions]
   316	  \label{lem:cl-func-prod}
   317	  Let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \ldots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that
   318	  $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   319	  Suppose that, for each $j\in\{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$, $L^{(j)}$ is an
   320	  $\ell_j$-level conditionally linear function on $V^{(j)}$.
   321	  Then the direct sum $L = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   322	  function over $V$ for $\ell = \max_j \{\ell_j\}$, where $L$ is defined by
   323	  \begin{equation*}
   324	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m  L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   325	  \end{equation*}
   326	  for all $x = \sum_{j=1}^m x^{(j)} \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.

   329	\begin{proof}
   330	  It is easy to see that an $\ell$-level CL function is also $k$-level
   331	  conditionally linear for all $k \ge \ell$.
   332	  Hence, it suffices to prove the claim where $\ell_j = \ell$ for $j=1, 2,
   333	  \ldots, m$.
   334	
   335	  We prove the theorem by an induction on $\ell$.
   336	  For $\ell = 1$, the functions $L^{(j)}$ are linear and the claim follows by
   337	  the fact that the direct sum of linear maps is linear.
   338	
   339	  Assume now the theorem holds for conditionally linear functions of level at
   340	  most $\ell-1$ and $L^{(j)}$ are $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions
   341	  for $j=1, 2, ,\ldots, m$.
   342	  By definition, $L^{(j)}$ is the concatenation of conditionally linear
   343	  functions $L^{(j)}_{1}$ on $V^{(j)}_1$ and $\{ L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j} \}_{v_j}$
   344	  on $V^{(j)}_{>1}$ of levels $1$, and $\ell-1$ respectively.
   345	  Furthermore,
   346	  \begin{equation*}
   347	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)} (x^{(j)}) = \sum_{j=1}^m \Bigl( v_j +
   348	    L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   349	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr) \Bigr),
   350	  \end{equation*}
   351	  where $v_j = L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   352	    \Bigr)$.
   353	  By the induction hypothesis,
   354	  \begin{equation*}
   355	    L_{1} (x^{V_1}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   356	    \Bigr),\quad L_{>1,\, v} (x^{V_{>1}}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   357	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr)
   358	  \end{equation*}
   359	  are $1$-level and $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear respectively for $v =
   360	  \sum_j v_j$, $V_1 = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_1$, and $V_{>1} =
   361	  \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_{>1}$.
   362	  This proves that $L$ is $\ell$-level conditionally linear.
   363	\end{proof}

   365	\begin{lemma}
   366	  \label{lem:cl-dist-prod}
   367	  For each $i \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $L^{(i)}, R^{(i)} : V^{(i)} \to V^{(i)}$
   368	  be $\ell_i$-level conditionally linear functions and let $L, R: V \to V$ be the
   369	  direct sums $L = \bigoplus_i L_i$ and $R = \bigoplus_i R_i$, respectively, as
   370	  defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}.
   371	  Then the conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L, R}$ is the product
   372	  distribution $\prod_{i=1}^m \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ over $V \times V$.
   373	\end{lemma}
   374	
   375	\begin{proof}
   376		The distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ is the distribution over pairs $(L(x),R(x))$
   377	  where $x$ is sampled uniformly from $V \times V$.
   378	  By Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}, this is equivalent to the distribution over
   379	  pairs $\bigl( (L_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m, (R_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m \bigr)$ where $x$
   380	  is chosen uniformly at random from $V$.
   381	  This distribution is exactly the product of the distributions $
   382	  \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, m$.
   383	\end{proof}

   313	    (R : (ιU → K) → (ιV → K) → (ιV → K))

   325	theorem IsCondLinearOn.concat {ιU ιV : Type*} [Fintype ιU] [DecidableEq ιU]
   326	    [Fintype ιV] [DecidableEq ιV] {ell k : ℕ}
   327	    {L : (ιU → K) → (ιU → K)}
   328	    {R : (ιU → K) → (ιV → K) → (ιV → K)}
   329	    (hL : IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset ιU) k L)
   330	    (hR : ∀ u : ιU → K, u ∈ Set.range L →
   331	      IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset ιV) ell (R u)) :
   332	    IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset (ιU ⊕ ιV)) (k + ell)
   333	      (condLinearConcat L R) := by
   334	  classical
   335	  rcases hL with ⟨tL, htL, htL_eval⟩
   336	  let rTerm : (ιU → K) → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ιV) ell := fun u =>
   337	    if hu : u ∈ Set.range L then Classical.choose (hR u hu)
   338	    else CondLinearTerm.zeroOfLevel ell
   339	  have hr_supported (u : ιU → K) :
   340	      CondLinearTerm.supportedOn (rTerm u) (Finset.univ : Finset ιV) := by
   341	    by_cases hu : u ∈ Set.range L
   342	    · simp only [rTerm, dif_pos hu]
   343	      exact (Classical.choose_spec (hR u hu)).1
   344	    · simp only [rTerm, dif_neg hu]
   345	      exact CondLinearTerm.zeroOfLevel_supportedOn ell Finset.univ

   347	      CondLinearTerm.eval (rTerm u) = R u := by
   348	    simp only [rTerm, dif_pos hu]
   349	    exact (Classical.choose_spec (hR u hu)).2
   350	  rw [Nat.add_comm k ell]
   351	  refine ⟨CondLinearTerm.concat rTerm 0 tL, ?_, ?_⟩
   352	  · have hsupport := CondLinearTerm.concat_supportedOn
   353	      (acc := (0 : ιU → K)) htL hr_supported
   354	    have huniv :
   355	        (Finset.univ : Finset ιU).map Function.Embedding.inl ∪
   356	            (Finset.univ : Finset ιV).map Function.Embedding.inr =
   357	          (Finset.univ : Finset (ιU ⊕ ιV)) := by
   358	      ext i
   359	      cases i <;> simp
   360	    simpa only [huniv] using hsupport
   361	  · funext x
   362	    rw [CondLinearTerm.eval_concat]
   363	    simp only [zero_add]
   364	    rw [congrFun htL_eval (fun i => x (.inl i))]
   365	    rw [hr_eval (L (fun i => x (.inl i))) ⟨_, rfl⟩]
   366	    rfl

190	  First consider the base case $\ell=1$.
   191	  Since $L_{<1} = 0$, we omit the mentioning of the prefix $u \in L_{<1}(V)$.
   192	  Define $L_{\leq 1} = L$, the factor space $V_1 = V$, and the linear map $L_1 =
   193	  L$.
   194	  It is straightforward to verify that the conditions in the lemma hold for
   195	  these choices of linear maps and spaces.
   196	  
   197	  Now, assume that the lemma holds for CL functions of level at most $\ell - 1$,
   198	  and we prove the lemma for $\ell$-level CL functions.
   199	  By definition, an $\ell$-level CL function $L$ can be written as
   200	  \begin{equation*}
   201	  	L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})
   202	  \end{equation*}
   203	  for some linear map $L_1 : V_1 \to V_1$ and a family of $(\ell-1)$-level CL
   204	  functions
   205	  \begin{equation*}
   206	    \bigl \{ L_{>1,\, v} : V_{>1} \to V_{>1} \bigr \}_{\, v \in L_1(V_1)}
   207	  \end{equation*}
   208	  where $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ are complementary register subspaces of $V$.
   209	  Next, using the inductive hypothesis on the $(\ell-1)$-level CL function
   210	  $L_{>1,\, v}$ we get that for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$ and all $k \in \{1, 2,
   211	  \ldots, \ell-1\}$ there exist $k$-th marginal functions $L'_{v,\, \le k}:
   212	  V_{>1} \to V_{>1}$, $k$-th factor spaces $V'_{v,\, k,\, u}$, and $k$-th linear
   213	  maps $L'_{v,\, k,\, u}$ of $L_{>1,\, v}$ with prefix $u \in L'_{v,\,
   214	    <k}(V_{>1})$ such that the conditions of the lemma for $L_{>1,\, v}$ hold.
   215	  
   216	  Define the marginal functions $L_{\le k} : V \to V$, factor spaces
   217	  $V_{k,\, u}$ and linear maps $L_{k,\, u}$ for $L$ as follows.
   218	  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
   219	  \item Define $L_{\le 1} = L_1$ and the first factor space to be $V_1$;
   220	  \item For all $k \in \{2, 3, \ldots, \ell\}$, define
   221	    \begin{equation}
   222	      \label{eq:cl-k-def}
   223	      L_{\le k}: x \mapsto x^{L_1} + L'_{x^{L_1},\, <k} (x^{V_{>1}})
   224	      \quad\text{for } x\in V;
   225	    \end{equation}
   226		\item For all $k \in \{2, 3, \ldots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{< k}(V)$, define
   227	    $V_{k,\, u} = V'_{v,\, k-1,\, w}$ and $L_{k,\, u} = L'_{v,\, k-1,\, w}$
   228	    where $v = u^{V_1} \in L_{1}(V_{1})$ and $w = u^{V_{>1}} \in L'_{v,< k-1}(V_{> 1})$.
   229	  \end{enumerate}
   230	  We verify that the conditions of the lemma are satisfied.
   231	  Since $L'_{v,\, < k}$ is by assumption a $(k-1)$-level CL function on $V_{>
   232	    1}$, we get that $L_{\leq k}$ is a $k$-level CL function on $V$ from
   233	  \cref{eq:cl-k-def}, establishing \cref{enu:cl-k-cl}.
   234	  By the induction hypothesis, we have for all $v\in L_1(V_1)$ and $y \in
   235	  V_{>1}$,
   236	  \begin{equation}
   237	    \label{eq:cl-k-1}
   238	    V_{>1} = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell-1}
   239	    V'_{\smash{v,\, i, \, y^{L'_{v,\, <i}}}},
   240	  \end{equation}
   241	  which implies that for all $x \in V$ and $v = x^{L_1}$,
   242	  \begin{equation*}
   243	    V = V_1 \oplus \Big ( \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell-1}
   244	    V'_{\smash{v,\, i, \, x^{L'_{v,\, <i}}}} \Big)
   245	    = V_1 \oplus \Big (\bigoplus_{i=2}^{\ell} V_{i,\, x^{L_{<i}}} \Big)
   246	    = \bigoplus_{i=1}^\ell V_{i,\, x^{L_{<i}}}\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  The first equality follows from \cref{eq:cl-k-1} while the second and third
   249	  equalities follow from the definition of $V_{k,\, u}$.
   250	  This establishes \cref{enu:cl-space-sum}.
   251	
   252	  Next, we have that for all $x \in V$, $v = x^{L_1}$, and $k \in
   253	  \{1,2,\ldots,\ell\}$,
   254	  \begin{align}
   255	    \label{eq:cl-last-ell}
   256	    L_{\leq k}(x)
   257	    & = v + L'_{v,\, <k} (x^{V_{>1}}) \\
   258	    & = v + \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} x^{L'_{v,\, i}}
   259	    = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} x^{L_{i}}, \label{eq:cl-last-ell2}
   260	  \end{align}
   261	  where $L'_{v,\, i}$ is the $i$-th linear map of $L_{>1,\, v}$ with prefix
   262	  $L'_{v,\, <i}(x)$ and $L_i$ is the $i$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix
   263	  $L_{<i}(x)$.
   264	  The second equality follows from the inductive hypothesis applied to $L'_{v,\,
   265	    <k}$ and the third equality follows from the definition of $L_{i}$.
   266	  Line~\eqref{eq:cl-last-ell2} implies \cref{enu:cl-map-sum} of the lemma.
   267	  
   268	  Finally, \Cref{enu:cl-last-ell} follows from~\eqref{eq:cl-last-ell} where we
   269	  set $k = \ell$ and observe that $L'_{x^{L_1},\, \le \ell-1}$ is equal to
   270	  $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ by the inductive hypothesis.
   271	  This shows that $L_{\le k}$, $V_{k,\, u}$, and $L_{k,\, u}$ satisfy the
   272	  conditions of the lemma and completes the induction.
   273	\end{proof}

   275	We note that the marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given
   276	CL function $L$ may not be unique; for example, consider the identity function
   277	on a linear space $V = \F^n$.
   278	This is clearly a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a
   279	$k$-level CL function for $k \in \{2, \ldots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition
   280	of $V$ into factor spaces.
   281	
   282	\begin{lemma}
   283	  \label{lem:cl-concat}
   284	  Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces.
   285	  Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   286	  function on $V$ for each $u \in L(U)$.
   287	  Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$ defined as
   288	  \begin{equation*}
   289	    T (x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)} (x^V)
   290	  \end{equation*}
   291	  is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U\oplus V$.
   292	\end{lemma}
   293	
   294	\begin{proof}
   295	  We prove the claim by induction on $k$.
   296	  The case $k = 0$ follows from the Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   297	  Assume that the lemma holds for $L$ being at most $(k-1)$-level.
   298	  By Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, there are complementary register subspaces
   299	  $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$, a linear function $L_1$ on $U_1$, and a family of
   300	  $(k-1)$-level CL functions $L_{>1,\, v}$ for $v \in L_1(U_1)$ such that
   301	  \begin{equation*}
   302	    L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}).
   303	  \end{equation*}
   304	  For all $x^{L_1}$, define the function $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ on $U_{>1} \oplus V$ as
   305	  \begin{equation*}
   306	    T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1} \oplus V}) = L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}) +
   307	    R_{x^{L_1} + x^{L_{>1}}}(x^V),
   308	  \end{equation*}
   309	  the concatenation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ and $\{ R_{L(x^U)} \}_{x^{L_{>1}}}$
   310	  where $L_{>1}$ is the shorthand notation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$.
   311	  By the induction hypothesis, $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ is $(k+\ell-1)$-level
   312	  conditionally linear.
   313	  The lemma follows from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   314	\end{proof}
   315	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of CL functions]
   316	  \label{lem:cl-func-prod}
   317	  Let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \ldots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that
   318	  $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   319	  Suppose that, for each $j\in\{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$, $L^{(j)}$ is an
   320	  $\ell_j$-level conditionally linear function on $V^{(j)}$.
   321	  Then the direct sum $L = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   322	  function over $V$ for $\ell = \max_j \{\ell_j\}$, where $L$ is defined by
   323	  \begin{equation*}
   324	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m  L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   325	  \end{equation*}
   326	  for all $x = \sum_{j=1}^m x^{(j)} \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   327	\end{lemma}
   328	
   329	\begin{proof}
   330	  It is easy to see that an $\ell$-level CL function is also $k$-level
   331	  conditionally linear for all $k \ge \ell$.
   332	  Hence, it suffices to prove the claim where $\ell_j = \ell$ for $j=1, 2,
   333	  \ldots, m$.
   334	
   335	  We prove the theorem by an induction on $\ell$.
   336	  For $\ell = 1$, the functions $L^{(j)}$ are linear and the claim follows by
   337	  the fact that the direct sum of linear maps is linear.
   338	
   339	  Assume now the theorem holds for conditionally linear functions of level at
   340	  most $\ell-1$ and $L^{(j)}$ are $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions
   341	  for $j=1, 2, ,\ldots, m$.
   342	  By definition, $L^{(j)}$ is the concatenation of conditionally linear
   343	  functions $L^{(j)}_{1}$ on $V^{(j)}_1$ and $\{ L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j} \}_{v_j}$
   344	  on $V^{(j)}_{>1}$ of levels $1$, and $\ell-1$ respectively.
   345	  Furthermore,
   346	  \begin{equation*}
   347	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)} (x^{(j)}) = \sum_{j=1}^m \Bigl( v_j +
   348	    L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   349	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr) \Bigr),
   350	  \end{equation*}
   351	  where $v_j = L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   352	    \Bigr)$.
   353	  By the induction hypothesis,
   354	  \begin{equation*}
   355	    L_{1} (x^{V_1}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   356	    \Bigr),\quad L_{>1,\, v} (x^{V_{>1}}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   357	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr)
   358	  \end{equation*}
   359	  are $1$-level and $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear respectively for $v =
   360	  \sum_j v_j$, $V_1 = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_1$, and $V_{>1} =
   361	  \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_{>1}$.
   362	  This proves that $L$ is $\ell$-level conditionally linear.
   363	\end{proof}

   365	\begin{lemma}
   366	  \label{lem:cl-dist-prod}
   367	  For each $i \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $L^{(i)}, R^{(i)} : V^{(i)} \to V^{(i)}$
   368	  be $\ell_i$-level conditionally linear functions and let $L, R: V \to V$ be the
   369	  direct sums $L = \bigoplus_i L_i$ and $R = \bigoplus_i R_i$, respectively, as
   370	  defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}.
   371	  Then the conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L, R}$ is the product
   372	  distribution $\prod_{i=1}^m \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ over $V \times V$.
   373	\end{lemma}
   374	
   375	\begin{proof}
   376		The distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ is the distribution over pairs $(L(x),R(x))$
   377	  where $x$ is sampled uniformly from $V \times V$.
   378	  By Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}, this is equivalent to the distribution over
   379	  pairs $\bigl( (L_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m, (R_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m \bigr)$ where $x$
   380	  is chosen uniformly at random from $V$.
   381	  This distribution is exactly the product of the distributions $
   382	  \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, m$.
   383	\end{proof}

1	# Blueprint Style Guide & Lessons Learned
     2	
     3	## Core Philosophy
     4	The blueprint is a **bridge between the mathematics and the Lean formalization**. A reader should be able to read a blueprint entry and immediately understand the corresponding Lean declaration. Conversely, someone reading the Lean code should find the blueprint proof sketch faithful to what the code actually does.
     5	
     6	## General Principles
     7	1. **Blueprint ↔ Lean must match.** Every `\lean{X}` tag must correspond to an actual Lean declaration. Every proof sketch must match what the Lean proof actually does — not a hand-wavy version of it.
     8	2. **Standalone.** `blueprint/` and any slides are independent — no cross-references, no shared files. Each has its own macros, its own `references.bib`.
     9	3. **Mathematical language only — zero Lean jargon.** No Lean identifiers in prose (no `selfImprovement_step`, no `PastingLemma.aux`, no `rintro ⟨X, hX⟩`). The `\lean{...}` tag is the link; the body text is standard mathematics. If you can't say it in math, rewrite it.
    10	4. **No filler prose.** Only precise definitions, theorem statements, and proof sketches. No "this is important because..." or "the self-improvement step governs the induction...".
    11	5. **Cite non-trivial things.** Basic definitions don't need citations. Important results and non-obvious definitions should cite the source paper.
    12	6. **Don't invent terminology or notation.** Don't create ad-hoc notation when standard notation exists. Don't name things that the literature doesn't name.
    13	7. **Match Lean's theorem/lemma/def exactly.** If Lean says `theorem X`, use `\begin{theorem}`. If Lean says `lemma X`, use `\begin{lemma}`. `\begin{proposition}` is allowed in blueprint prose when it improves mathematical readability, but still map it to an actual Lean `theorem`/`lemma` declaration via `\lean{...}`. Label prefix: `thm:` for theorem, `lem:` for lemma, `def:` for definition, `prop:` for proposition.
    14	
    15	### Remark On Mathematical Prose
    16	
    17	Blueprint entries should read as mathematical exposition, not as progress
    18	reports. The mathematical argument should determine the order of the prose:
    19	introduce the notation, state the assertion, give the proof or calculation, and
    20	then record Lean references through the usual blueprint tags. Lean declarations,
    21	file paths, and proof-status information should not become the visible structure
    22	of the paragraph. When referring to a source article, cite it bibliographically
    23	rather than relying on an uncited reference to the article.
    24	
    25	Use displayed formulae when the formula benefits from visual separation, and
    26	keep short scalar definitions or elementary inequalities inline when the
    27	sentence reads better that way. As in ordinary mathematical writing, displayed
    28	formulae should be punctuated as part of the sentences in which they occur.
    29	
    30	## Proof Sketches Must Match Lean
    31	This is the most important rule. Every proof in the blueprint must faithfully describe what the Lean proof does:
    32	
    33	- **Reference the actual lemmas used.** If the Lean proof calls `LDT.selfImprovement`, the blueprint proof should say "By Lemma X.Y (self-improvement)..." and list it in `\uses`.
    34	- **Do not use `\cref` or `\Cref`.** The blueprint does not load `cleveref`.
    35	  Spell out the kind of object and use ordinary references, for example
    36	  `Lemma~\ref{lem:self-improvement}` or `Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}`.
    37	- **Describe the actual proof structure.** If Lean does induction on a parameter, say so. If Lean uses a specific decomposition, name it.
    38	- **Don't hand-wave where Lean is specific.** "Standard argument" is not acceptable if Lean uses three specific lemmas. Name them.
    39	- **Don't be more specific than Lean.** If Lean uses `simp` to close a goal, a one-line sketch is fine.
    40	- **`\uses` in proofs must be accurate.** Only list what the proof actually uses, not what the statement mentions.
    41	
    42	## Source-Labelled Statements And Conditional Helpers
    43	
    44	If a blueprint theorem, lemma, or proposition carries a source label from the
    45	paper, the linked Lean declaration must state the same theorem, up to faithful
    46	formal encoding of the paper's domain.  Do not use `\lean{...}` and `\leanok`
    47	on the source-labelled statement to point to a conditional helper whose
    48	additional assumptions supply an unproved part of the paper proof.
    49	Changing the Lean statement away from `references/ldt-paper/` is strongly
    50	discouraged unless faithful formal encoding or a documented mathematical
    51	necessity requires it; the blueprint should make any such necessity explicit.
    52	
    53	Boundary hypotheses such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
    54	positivity of parameters, and denominator nonvanishing may be faithful when
    55	they express the mathematical domain that the paper leaves implicit.  By
    56	contrast, bridge inputs, residual data, repair hypotheses, producer
    57	assumptions, proof-obligation inputs, or package assumptions are proof debt.
    58	They must not be added to a source-labelled theorem statement.  If such data is
    59	still unproved, the source-labelled Lean theorem should keep the source-shaped
    60	statement and carry a tracked `sorry`, or the missing assertion should appear
    61	as the lowest named internal obligation with a tracked `sorry`.  A separately
    62	named conditional helper should not be introduced as a repair pattern.  If one
    63	already contains substantial proof content, it may remain temporarily only as
    64	quarantine: it needs a paper source, a tracking issue, and a discharge or
    65	deletion plan.  The blueprint should leave the paper theorem unmarked as
    66	proof-complete until the source-faithful Lean statement has a source-faithful
    67	proof.
    68	
    69	If a Lean theorem proves only a restricted version of a source theorem, the
    70	blueprint entry carrying `\leanok` must state that restriction in the theorem
    71	statement itself.  It must not be cited as the unrestricted source theorem.
    72	When the only Lean declaration available for a source label has extra
    73	non-paper assumptions, remove the `\leanok` claim from the source-labelled
    74	entry or move the restricted statement to a separate Lean-only entry.  The
    75	unrestricted paper theorem remains unformalized until a Lean statement with
    76	the source's hypothesis set exists.
    77	
    78	## Notation Consistency
    79	Notation must be **internally consistent** across the entire blueprint and **close to what the Lean code expresses**:
    80	
    81	- **Indices**: 0-indexed where matching `Fin n` in Lean
    82	- **Finite fields / alphabets**: use standard notation for the alphabet $\Sigma$ and finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$
    83	- **Measurements**: use standard quantum measurement notation (projective measurements, POVMs)
    84	- **Strategies**: quantum strategies for nonlocal games should use standard notation from the literature
    85	- **Expansion**: use standard notation for graph expansion parameters
    86	- **Macros** (in `macros/common.tex`): define project-specific macros and use them consistently
    87	
    88	The original reference controls notation whenever it gives a usable convention.
    89	If the blueprint needs a different symbol, index convention, or name in order to
    90	match Lean, introduce it explicitly and relate it to the paper notation in the
    91	same paragraph.  Do not let a `\lean{...}` tag, a Lean namespace, or a file name
    92	be the only explanation of a changed term.
    93	
    94	When a public Lean declaration is a formalization-only auxiliary lemma, the
    95	blueprint should say so before listing the declaration.  The surrounding prose
    96	should identify the paper theorem, equation, or construction that the auxiliary
    97	lemma supports, and should avoid making the auxiliary name look like a named
    98	result from the source article.
    99	
   100	## What NOT to Put in the Blueprint
   101	- **Lean identifier names in math text.** Write "the self-improvement lemma", never "the `selfImprovement` step". The `\lean{LDT.selfImprovement}` tag handles the linking.
   102	- **Implementation details.** Don't say "bundled as an element of the Euclidean space" or "using `EuclideanSpace.equiv`". Describe the mathematical object.
   103	- **Ad-hoc notation.** Don't invent superscripts or subscripts to distinguish from existing notation. Use standard conventions.
   104	- **Function-call syntax.** Use mathematical notation, not programming notation.
   105	- **Redundant definitions.** If two blueprint definitions describe the same mathematical object, consolidate them. Each definition should introduce genuinely new mathematical content.
   106	- **Lean namespace prefixes in prose.** Don't write "the `LDT.PastingLemma`" — write "the pasting lemma".
   107	
   108	## Banned AI/Software Language (enforced in both blueprint AND Lean code)
   109	The blueprint reads as a **mathematical document**, not software documentation. The following patterns are banned in ALL reader-facing text (section titles, theorem names, proof sketches, remarks, chapter preambles) and in ALL Lean docstrings, comments, and section names:
   110	
   111	### Banned terms → replacements:
   112	| Banned | Use instead |
   113	|--------|------------|
   114	| "Assembly" (as section/chapter title) | "Proof of [theorem]", "Construction", "Composition" |
   115	| "Pipeline" | "reduction", "construction", "proof chain" |
   116	| "Bridge" (as noun for a connection) | "connection", name by mathematical content |
   117	| "Handoff" / "hand off" | "transition", "continuation", or drop entirely |
   118	| "In this blueprint" / "Within this blueprint" | "here", "in what follows", or omit |
   119	| "Honest" (as adjective for rigorous) | "exact", "faithful", "unconditional", "complete" |
   120	| "Glue layer" | "intermediate construction", "connecting results" |
   121	| "Re-export" / "reexport" | "provides", "re-states" |
   122	| "Wiring" / "wire up" | "connecting", "composing", "combining" |
   123	| "Package" (as noun for a data bundle) | "form", "data", "structure" |
   124	| "Sorry-free" | acceptable only in Lean-specific technical context |
   125	
   126	### Additional rules:
   127	- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
   128	- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
   129	- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.
   130	
   131	## `\uses` Dependency Guidelines
   132	- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.
   133	- **Proof `\uses`**: list only what the proof *actually calls*. Don't list definitions unless the proof unfolds that definition.
   134	- **Never self-reference**: a proof's `\uses` must NOT include the label of the theorem it proves.
   135	
   136	## Recording Formalization-Only Lemmas
   137	Some Lean lemmas are genuine proof infrastructure rather than named statements
   138	from the original papers. These must be traceable without making the blueprint
   139	look as if the paper stated them.
   140	
   141	- If a declaration directly formalizes a paper or blueprint statement, record
   142	  it as usual with `\lean{...}` on that statement and cite the relevant source.
   143	- If a public declaration is an auxiliary lemma introduced only for the Lean
   144	  proof, make that status explicit. Its Lean docstring should say that it is a
   145	  formalization-only auxiliary lemma and should name the nearby paper equation,
   146	  line range, or blueprint result it supports.
   147	- If such an auxiliary declaration is important enough to be referenced from
   148	  the blueprint, give it a clearly subordinate blueprint node, for example
   149	  `[Formalization support for ...]`, and state in the first sentence that the
   150	  lemma is not a named statement of the paper but isolates a step used in the
   151	  Lean proof.
   152	- Connect auxiliary nodes to the corresponding result from the paper with `\uses{...}` from
   153	  the proof that actually calls them. Do not add them only to silence a sync
   154	  warning; the dependency edge should explain where the auxiliary result is
   155	  used.
   156	- Do not mark an auxiliary node with proof-level `\leanok` unless its Lean proof
   157	  is complete and `#print axioms` has no `sorryAx`. Statement-level `\leanok`
   158	  is acceptable only when the Lean statement is intentionally recorded but the
   159	  proof remains tracked as incomplete.
   160	
   161	## Blueprint Structure
   162	- `content.tex` is a router: `\input{chapter/ch01_intro}` etc.
   163	- Each chapter is a separate file in `chapter/`
   164	- Definitions/theorems numbered within chapters: `\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[chapter]`
   165	
   166	## Lean Blueprint Macros
   167	- `\lean{Namespace.DeclName}` — links to Lean declaration
   168	- `\leanok` — context-sensitive marker; see "Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`" below
   169	- `\uses{label1, label2}` — declares dependency edges for the graph
   170	- `\notready` — marks as not ready for formalization (orange in graph)
   171	- `\mathlibok` — already in Mathlib (dark green in graph; see legend note below)
   172	
   173	### Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`
   174	
   175	`\leanok` is context-sensitive for human review and graph interpretation. The same macro is used for two different claims, so reviewers should read it by placement rather than by raw token count.
   176	
   177	**Statement-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside a `theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, or `definition` environment, on its own line immediately after `\lean{...}`. It says that the corresponding Lean declaration exists and that its statement matches the blueprint or paper statement. It does **not** say that the Lean proof already exists or is complete. For definitions, this is the only `\leanok` marker.
   178	
   179	**Proof-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside the matching `proof` environment, preferably as the first line after `\begin{proof}`. The canonical current placement is the theorem `thm:commutativity-points` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch08_commutativity.tex:8-19`, where the statement block has `\leanok` immediately after `\lean{...}` and the proof block begins with another `\leanok`. This marker says that the Lean proof is complete and free of unresolved `sorry` or unjustified project-level `axiom` shortcuts. In particular, `#print axioms <decl>` must show no `sorryAx`, and the declaration must satisfy the broader blocker rules in the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference and [`docs/project_conventions.md`](project_conventions.md).
   180	
   181	A theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary node is **fully formalized in Lean if and only if it has both markers**: statement-level `\leanok` in the statement block and proof-level `\leanok` in the proof block. Statement-level without proof-level means “the statement has been transcribed and matched, but the proof is not yet certified complete.” Definitions have no proof block, so statement-level `\leanok` alone is enough there.

275	We note that the marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given
   276	CL function $L$ may not be unique; for example, consider the identity function
   277	on a linear space $V = \F^n$.
   278	This is clearly a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a
   279	$k$-level CL function for $k \in \{2, \ldots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition
   280	of $V$ into factor spaces.
   281	
   282	\begin{lemma}
   283	  \label{lem:cl-concat}
   284	  Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces.
   285	  Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   286	  function on $V$ for each $u \in L(U)$.
   287	  Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$ defined as
   288	  \begin{equation*}
   289	    T (x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)} (x^V)
   290	  \end{equation*}
   291	  is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U\oplus V$.
   292	\end{lemma}
   293	
   294	\begin{proof}
   295	  We prove the claim by induction on $k$.
   296	  The case $k = 0$ follows from the Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   297	  Assume that the lemma holds for $L$ being at most $(k-1)$-level.
   298	  By Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, there are complementary register subspaces
   299	  $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$, a linear function $L_1$ on $U_1$, and a family of
   300	  $(k-1)$-level CL functions $L_{>1,\, v}$ for $v \in L_1(U_1)$ such that
   301	  \begin{equation*}
   302	    L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}).
   303	  \end{equation*}
   304	  For all $x^{L_1}$, define the function $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ on $U_{>1} \oplus V$ as
   305	  \begin{equation*}
   306	    T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1} \oplus V}) = L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}) +
   307	    R_{x^{L_1} + x^{L_{>1}}}(x^V),
   308	  \end{equation*}
   309	  the concatenation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ and $\{ R_{L(x^U)} \}_{x^{L_{>1}}}$
   310	  where $L_{>1}$ is the shorthand notation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$.
   311	  By the induction hypothesis, $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ is $(k+\ell-1)$-level
   312	  conditionally linear.
   313	  The lemma follows from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   314	\end{proof}
   315	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of CL functions]
   316	  \label{lem:cl-func-prod}
   317	  Let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \ldots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that
   318	  $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   319	  Suppose that, for each $j\in\{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$, $L^{(j)}$ is an
   320	  $\ell_j$-level conditionally linear function on $V^{(j)}$.
   321	  Then the direct sum $L = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   322	  function over $V$ for $\ell = \max_j \{\ell_j\}$, where $L$ is defined by
   323	  \begin{equation*}
   324	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m  L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   325	  \end{equation*}
   326	  for all $x = \sum_{j=1}^m x^{(j)} \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   327	\end{lemma}
   328	
   329	\begin{proof}
   330	  It is easy to see that an $\ell$-level CL function is also $k$-level
   331	  conditionally linear for all $k \ge \ell$.
   332	  Hence, it suffices to prove the claim where $\ell_j = \ell$ for $j=1, 2,
   333	  \ldots, m$.
   334	
   335	  We prove the theorem by an induction on $\ell$.
   336	  For $\ell = 1$, the functions $L^{(j)}$ are linear and the claim follows by
   337	  the fact that the direct sum of linear maps is linear.
   338	
   339	  Assume now the theorem holds for conditionally linear functions of level at
   340	  most $\ell-1$ and $L^{(j)}$ are $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions
   341	  for $j=1, 2, ,\ldots, m$.
   342	  By definition, $L^{(j)}$ is the concatenation of conditionally linear
   343	  functions $L^{(j)}_{1}$ on $V^{(j)}_1$ and $\{ L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j} \}_{v_j}$
   344	  on $V^{(j)}_{>1}$ of levels $1$, and $\ell-1$ respectively.
   345	  Furthermore,
   346	  \begin{equation*}
   347	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)} (x^{(j)}) = \sum_{j=1}^m \Bigl( v_j +
   348	    L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   349	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr) \Bigr),
   350	  \end{equation*}
   351	  where $v_j = L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   352	    \Bigr)$.
   353	  By the induction hypothesis,
   354	  \begin{equation*}
   355	    L_{1} (x^{V_1}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   356	    \Bigr),\quad L_{>1,\, v} (x^{V_{>1}}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   357	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr)
   358	  \end{equation*}
   359	  are $1$-level and $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear respectively for $v =
   360	  \sum_j v_j$, $V_1 = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_1$, and $V_{>1} =
   361	  \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_{>1}$.
   362	  This proves that $L$ is $\ell$-level conditionally linear.
   363	\end{proof}

   365	\begin{lemma}
   366	  \label{lem:cl-dist-prod}
   367	  For each $i \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $L^{(i)}, R^{(i)} : V^{(i)} \to V^{(i)}$
   368	  be $\ell_i$-level conditionally linear functions and let $L, R: V \to V$ be the
   369	  direct sums $L = \bigoplus_i L_i$ and $R = \bigoplus_i R_i$, respectively, as
   370	  defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}.
   371	  Then the conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L, R}$ is the product
   372	  distribution $\prod_{i=1}^m \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ over $V \times V$.
   373	\end{lemma}
   374	
   375	\begin{proof}
   376		The distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ is the distribution over pairs $(L(x),R(x))$
   377	  where $x$ is sampled uniformly from $V \times V$.
   378	  By Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}, this is equivalent to the distribution over
   379	  pairs $\bigl( (L_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m, (R_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m \bigr)$ where $x$
   380	  is chosen uniformly at random from $V$.
   381	  This distribution is exactly the product of the distributions $
   382	  \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, m$.
   383	\end{proof}

1	\section{Types}
     2	\label{sec:types}
     3	
     4	We augment the definition of conditionally linear functions with a construct
     5	we call \emph{types}.
     6	A type~$\tvar$ is an element of a \emph{type set} $\type$, and a $\type$-typed
     7	family of conditionally linear functions is a collection
     8	$\{L_\tvar\}_{\tvar\in\type}$ containing a CL function $L_\tvar$ for each
     9	type~$\tvar\in\type$.
    10	The utility of this definition is that it allows us to define another object,
    11	namely conditionally linear distributions parameterized by an undirected graph
    12	$G = (\type, E)$ on the set of types known as a \emph{type graph}.
    13	Given two $\type$-typed families of conditionally linear functions
    14	$\{L_\lvar\}_{\lvar\in\type}, \{R_\rvar\}_{\rvar\in\type}$, the $(\type,
    15	G)$-typed conditionally linear distribution corresponding to them is the
    16	distribution which samples a pair of types $(\lvar, \rvar)$ uniformly at random
    17	from the edges of~$G$ (with each endpoint having equal probability as being
    18	chosen for $\lvar$ or $\rvar$, respectively) and then samples $(x, y)$ from
    19	$\mu_{L_\lvar,\, R_\rvar}$.
    20	The output is the pair $( (\lvar, x), (\rvar, y) )$.
    21	
    22	The normal form verifiers we present in the paper frequently use typed CL
    23	distributions to sample their questions, rather than untyped CL distributions.
    24	Types allow us to model the parts of their question distributions which are
    25	unstructured and unsuitable for being sampled from CL distributions.
    26	A common use of types is to allow the verifier to use previously defined games
    27	as subroutines.
    28	Here, the type helps indicate which subroutine the verifier selects, and an edge
    29	in the type graph between two different types allows us to introduce a test that
    30	cross-checks the results of one subroutine with the results of another.
    31	
    32	Finally, we show how to convert any typed CL distribution into an equivalent (in
    33	the precise sense defined below) untyped CL distribution with two additional
    34	levels, a technique we call \emph{detyping}.
    35	This entails showing how to ``simulate'' the \emph{graph distribution} of $G =
    36	(\type, E)$, i.e.\ the uniform distribution on its edges, using an untyped CL
    37	distribution.
    38	The simulation we give is based on rejection sampling and is only approximate:
    39	its quality degrades exponentially with the number of types in~$\type$.
    40	As a result, we will ensure throughout the paper that all type sets we consider
    41	are of a small, in fact generally constant, size.
    42	
    43	This section is organized as follows.
    44	In \cref{sec:typed-samplers} we define typed variants of CL distributions,
    45	samplers, deciders, and verifiers.
    46	In \cref{sec:graph-dist} we define a CL distribution which samples from the
    47	graph distribution of a given graph $G = (\type, E)$.
    48	In \cref{sec:detype} we define a canonical way to detype typed samplers,
    49	deciders, and verifiers using the graph sampler from \cref{sec:graph-dist}.
    50	We then prove the main result of the section, \cref{lem:detyping-verifiers},
    51	which relates the value of the detyped normal form verifier to the value of
    52	the original typed verifier.

    54	\subsection{Typed samplers, deciders, and verifiers}
    55	\label{sec:typed-samplers}
    56	
    57	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear functions]
    58	  Let $\type$ be a finite set and $V$ be $\F^n$ for some integer $n \geq 0$.
    59	  A \emph{$\type$-typed family of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions}
    60	  (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is a collection $\{L_\tvar\}_{\tvar \in \type}$
    61	  such that, for each $\tvar \in \type$, $L_\tvar$ is an $\ell$-level
    62	  conditionally linear function on~$V$.
    63	\end{definition}
    64	
    65	\begin{definition}[Graph distribution]
    66	  \label{def:graph-distribution}
    67	  Let $G = (U, E)$ be an undirected graph with vertex set $U$ and edge set~$E$.
    68	  Edges in~$E$ are written as multisets $\{u, v\}$ of two vertices; the case $u
    69	  = v$ represents a self-loop.
    70	  Suppose there are $m$ edges, $k$ of which are self-loops.
    71	  Then the \emph{graph distribution $\mu_G$ of~$G$} is the distribution over
    72	  $U\times U$ such that for every $(u, v)\in U\times U$,
    73	  \begin{equation*}
    74	    \mu_G(u, v) =
    75	    \begin{cases}
    76	      1/(2m-k) & \text{if $\{u, v\} \in E$},\\
    77	      0 & \text{otherwise}.
    78	    \end{cases}
    79	  \end{equation*}
    80	  This is identical to the uniform distribution over pairs $(u, v)\in U\times U$
    81	  such that $\{u, v\} \in E$.
    82	\end{definition}

    90	      R}^G$ corresponding to~$(L, R)$} is the distribution over pairs $( (\lvar,
    91	  x), (\rvar, y) )$, where $(\lvar, \rvar)$ is drawn from $\mu_G$ and $(x,y)$ is
    92	  drawn from $\mu_{L_\lvar,\, R_\rvar}$.
    93	\end{definition}

   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}
   962	
   963	
   964	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show
   966	that it is a (typed) CL distribution.
   967	The question types in the game $\game^\pauli$ are
   968	\begin{equation}
   969	  \label{eq:pauli-type}
   970	  \type^\pauli= \bigl( \{\Point, \ALine, \DLine, \Pauli, \Pair \} \times \{X,Z\} \bigr)
   971	  \cup \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair\}\;,
   972	\end{equation}
   973	where $\type^\ms$ is the question type set of the Magic Square game defined in
   974	Section~\ref{sec:ms}.
   975	
   976	
   977	
   978	
   979	Before presenting the CL functions of the Pauli basis test, we first give an
   980	intuitive description of the question distribution of the Pauli basis test: a
   981	pair of questions $((\tvar_\alice, x_\alice), (\tvar_\bob, x_\bob))$ in
   982	$\game^\pauli$ can be sampled via the following procedure:
   983	
   984	\begin{enumerate}
   985	\item Sample a pair of types by sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice, \tvar_\bob)$ of
   986	  the graph $G^\pauli$ given in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli} uniformly at
   987	  random (including the self-loops).
   988	\item Sample the following uniformly at random:
   989		\begin{enumerate}
   990		\item (\emph{Points}) $u_\xpt,u_\zpt \in \F_q^m$,
   991		\item (\emph{Directions}) $s \in \F_q$, $v \in \F_q^m$,
   992	  \item (\emph{Qubit basis for (anti-)commutation}) $r_\xpt,r_\zpt \in \F_q$.
   993		\end{enumerate}
   994	\item For $w \in \AB$ and $W\in\{X,Z\}$,
   995		\begin{enumerate}
   996	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W)$, then set $x_w = u_W$,
   997	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\ALine, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s)$, where $u_0 =
   998	    L^\lnf_{e_i}(u_W)$, with $i = \chi(s)$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-game} for
   999	    definition of $L^\lnf$ and $\chi(s)$),
  1000	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\DLine,W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s,v')$, where $i =
  1001	    \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^\lnf_{v'}(u_W)$,
  1002	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Constraint_i$ for some $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$, then set
  1003	    $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1004	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Variable_j$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,9\}$, then set $x_w
  1005	    = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1006	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Pair$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1007	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1008	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pauli, W)$, then set $x_w = 0$.
  1009		\end{enumerate}
  1010	\end{enumerate}

   120	  have hq : 0 < L.q := ldParams_q_pos L
   121	  have hqk : L.m * (L.q / L.m) = L.q := Nat.mul_div_cancel' L.hdvd
   122	  have hkpos : 0 < L.q / L.m := by
   123	    rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos (L.q / L.m) with h | h
   124	    · rw [h, Nat.mul_zero] at hqk
   125	      omega
   126	    · exact h
   127	  have hstep1 :
   128	      ((Finset.univ : Finset (ScalarQ L)).filter fun s => chiIndex L s = i).card
   129	        = ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin L.q)).filter
   130	            fun n => (n.val / (L.q / L.m)) % L.m = i.val).card := by

   137	    ext t
   138	    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range, Finset.mem_image,
   139	      Finset.mem_univ, true_and]
   140	    constructor
   141	    · rintro ⟨ht, hP⟩
   142	      exact ⟨⟨t, ht⟩, hP, rfl⟩
   143	    · rintro ⟨n, hP, rfl⟩
   144	      exact ⟨n.isLt, hP⟩

   146	      ((Finset.range L.q).filter fun t => (t / (L.q / L.m)) % L.m = i.val)

   148	    ext t
   149	    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range, Finset.mem_Ico]
   150	    constructor
   151	    · rintro ⟨htq, hP⟩
   152	      have hlt : t / (L.q / L.m) < L.m := by
   153	        rw [Nat.div_lt_iff_lt_mul hkpos]
   154	        omega
   155	      have hdiv : t / (L.q / L.m) = i.val := by
   156	        rwa [Nat.mod_eq_of_lt hlt] at hP

   160	        omega
   161	      have hexp : (i.val + 1) * (L.q / L.m)

   163	      rw [hdiv] at hle
   164	      omega
   165	    · rintro ⟨hlo, hhi⟩
   166	      have hexp : (i.val + 1) * (L.q / L.m)
   167	          = i.val * (L.q / L.m) + L.q / L.m := by ring

   170	        have h2 : t / (L.q / L.m) < i.val + 1 := by
   171	          rw [Nat.div_lt_iff_lt_mul hkpos]
   172	          omega
   173	        omega
   174	      refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
   175	      · have hbound : (i.val + 1) * (L.q / L.m) ≤ L.m * (L.q / L.m) :=
   176	          Nat.mul_le_mul_right _ i.isLt
   177	        omega
   178	      · rw [hdiv, Nat.mod_eq_of_lt i.isLt]

   180	      ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin L.q)).filter

   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238	
   239	
   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   197	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary: the linear map retaining the shared scalar
   198	coordinate and clearing every other coordinate. -/
   199	private def ldSeedLinear (P : LdParams) :
   200	    LdSpace P →ₗ[ScalarQ P] LdSpace P where
   201	  toFun x := fun i =>
   202	    match i with
   203	    | .inl (.inl _) => 0
   204	    | .inl (.inr _) => x (Sum.inl (Sum.inr ()))
   205	    | .inr _ => 0
   206	  map_add' x y := by
   207	    funext i
   208	    rcases i with (j | u) | j <;> simp
   209	  map_smul' c x := by
   210	    funext i
   211	    rcases i with (j | u) | j <;> simp

   213	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary: the linear map sending the point block to its
   214	canonical line representative in the fixed direction `v` and clearing every
   215	other coordinate. -/
   216	private noncomputable def ldPointCLLinear (P : LdParams) (v : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P) :
   217	    LdSpace P →ₗ[ScalarQ P] LdSpace P where
   218	  toFun x := fun i =>
   219	    match i with
   220	    | .inl (.inl j) => lineRepMap v (LdSpace.point x) j
   221	    | .inl (.inr _) => 0
   222	    | .inr _ => 0
   223	  map_add' x y := by
   224	    funext i
   225	    rcases i with (j | u) | j
   226	    · change lineRepMap v (LdSpace.point (x + y)) j = _
   227	      have hpoint : LdSpace.point (x + y) = LdSpace.point x + LdSpace.point y := rfl
   228	      rw [hpoint, map_add]
   229	      rfl
   230	    · simp
   231	    · simp
   232	  map_smul' c x := by
   233	    funext i
   234	    rcases i with (j | u) | j
   235	    · change lineRepMap v (LdSpace.point (c • x)) j = _
   236	      have hpoint : LdSpace.point (c • x) = c • LdSpace.point x := rfl
   237	      rw [hpoint, map_smul]
   238	      rfl
   239	    · simp
   240	    · simp

   242	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary: the linear map zeroing the first `i`
   243	coordinates of the direction block and clearing every other coordinate. -/
   244	private def ldDirectionCLLinear (P : LdParams) (i : Fin P.m) :
   245	    LdSpace P →ₗ[ScalarQ P] LdSpace P where
   246	  toFun x := fun k =>
   247	    match k with
   248	    | .inl (.inl _) => 0
   249	    | .inl (.inr _) => 0
   250	    | .inr j => prefixProjection i (LdSpace.direction x) j
   251	  map_add' x y := by
   252	    funext k
   253	    rcases k with (j | u) | j
   254	    · simp
   255	    · simp
   256	    · change prefixProjection i (LdSpace.direction (x + y)) j =
   257	        prefixProjection i (LdSpace.direction x) j +
   258	          prefixProjection i (LdSpace.direction y) j
   259	      by_cases h : j.val < i.val
   260	      · simp only [prefixProjection, if_pos h, add_zero]
   261	      · simp only [prefixProjection, if_neg h]
   262	        rfl
   263	  map_smul' c x := by
   264	    funext k
   265	    rcases k with (j | u) | j
   266	    · simp
   267	    · simp
   268	    · change prefixProjection i (LdSpace.direction (c • x)) j =
   269	        c • prefixProjection i (LdSpace.direction x) j
   270	      by_cases h : j.val < i.val
   271	      · simp only [prefixProjection, if_pos h, smul_zero]
   272	      · simp only [prefixProjection, if_neg h]
   273	        rfl

    36	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary equivalence splitting an ambient low-degree
    37	vector into its point, seed, and direction blocks. -/
    38	private def ldSpaceSplit (L : LdParams) :
    39	    LdSpace L ≃ ((Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) × ScalarQ L) × (Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) where
    40	  toFun z := ((LdSpace.point z, LdSpace.seed z), LdSpace.direction z)
    41	  invFun p := fun i =>
    42	    match i with
    43	    | .inl (.inl j) => p.1.1 j
    44	    | .inl (.inr _) => p.1.2
    45	    | .inr j => p.2 j
    46	  left_inv z := by
    47	    funext i
    48	    rcases i with (j | u) | j
    49	    · rfl
    50	    · cases u
    51	      rfl
    52	    · rfl
    53	  right_inv p := by
    54	    obtain ⟨⟨a, b⟩, c⟩ := p
    55	    rfl

   108	    chiIndex L s = i ↔

   113	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary lemma: every fiber of the coordinate index has
   114	exactly `q / m` elements.  This is the balance property used in
   115	`def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:34-59`, paper
   116	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`. -/
   117	private theorem card_chiIndex_fiber (L : LdParams) (i : Fin L.m) :
   118	    ((Finset.univ : Finset (ScalarQ L)).filter fun s => chiIndex L s = i).card
   119	      = L.q / L.m := by
   120	  have hq : 0 < L.q := ldParams_q_pos L
   121	  have hqk : L.m * (L.q / L.m) = L.q := Nat.mul_div_cancel' L.hdvd
   122	  have hkpos : 0 < L.q / L.m := by
   123	    rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos (L.q / L.m) with h | h
   124	    · rw [h, Nat.mul_zero] at hqk
   125	      omega
   126	    · exact h
   127	  have hstep1 :
   128	      ((Finset.univ : Finset (ScalarQ L)).filter fun s => chiIndex L s = i).card
   129	        = ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin L.q)).filter
   130	            fun n => (n.val / (L.q / L.m)) % L.m = i.val).card := by
   131	    refine Finset.card_equiv (binaryRepresentation L.model) fun s => ?_
   132	    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, chiIndex_eq_iff]
   133	  have hstep2 :
   134	      ((Finset.range L.q).filter fun t => (t / (L.q / L.m)) % L.m = i.val)
   135	        = ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin L.q)).filter
   136	            fun n => (n.val / (L.q / L.m)) % L.m = i.val).image Fin.val := by
   137	    ext t
   138	    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range, Finset.mem_image,
   139	      Finset.mem_univ, true_and]
   140	    constructor
   141	    · rintro ⟨ht, hP⟩
   142	      exact ⟨⟨t, ht⟩, hP, rfl⟩
   143	    · rintro ⟨n, hP, rfl⟩
   144	      exact ⟨n.isLt, hP⟩
   145	  have hstep3 :
   146	      ((Finset.range L.q).filter fun t => (t / (L.q / L.m)) % L.m = i.val)
   147	        = Finset.Ico (i.val * (L.q / L.m)) (i.val * (L.q / L.m) + L.q / L.m) := by
   148	    ext t
   149	    simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_range, Finset.mem_Ico]
   150	    constructor
   151	    · rintro ⟨htq, hP⟩
   152	      have hlt : t / (L.q / L.m) < L.m := by
   153	        rw [Nat.div_lt_iff_lt_mul hkpos]
   154	        omega
   155	      have hdiv : t / (L.q / L.m) = i.val := by
   156	        rwa [Nat.mod_eq_of_lt hlt] at hP
   157	      have hle : t / (L.q / L.m) * (L.q / L.m) ≤ t := Nat.div_mul_le_self t _
   158	      have hupper : t < (i.val + 1) * (L.q / L.m) := by
   159	        rw [← Nat.div_lt_iff_lt_mul hkpos, hdiv]
   160	        omega
   161	      have hexp : (i.val + 1) * (L.q / L.m)
   162	          = i.val * (L.q / L.m) + L.q / L.m := by ring
   163	      rw [hdiv] at hle
   164	      omega
   165	    · rintro ⟨hlo, hhi⟩
   166	      have hexp : (i.val + 1) * (L.q / L.m)
   167	          = i.val * (L.q / L.m) + L.q / L.m := by ring
   168	      have hdiv : t / (L.q / L.m) = i.val := by
   169	        have h1 : i.val ≤ t / (L.q / L.m) := (Nat.le_div_iff_mul_le hkpos).mpr hlo
   170	        have h2 : t / (L.q / L.m) < i.val + 1 := by
   171	          rw [Nat.div_lt_iff_lt_mul hkpos]
   172	          omega
   173	        omega
   174	      refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
   175	      · have hbound : (i.val + 1) * (L.q / L.m) ≤ L.m * (L.q / L.m) :=
   176	          Nat.mul_le_mul_right _ i.isLt
   177	        omega
   178	      · rw [hdiv, Nat.mod_eq_of_lt i.isLt]
   179	  rw [hstep1, ← Finset.card_image_of_injective
   180	      ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin L.q)).filter
   181	        fun n => (n.val / (L.q / L.m)) % L.m = i.val) Fin.val_injective,
   182	    ← hstep2, hstep3, Nat.card_Ico]
   183	  omega
